topics.title: moab33's Math Tips #2: Nice formula!
topics.text:
So, when I was cleaning up books yesterday, I came up with this problem:

I have $k$ books. $a$ are of one series and $b$ of another. The series do not overlap (a.k.a $a+b=k$). If I chose two books, what is the probability that both of the same series? (Either $a$ followed by $a$ or $b$ followed by $b$?)

Think for a minute before looking at this.

Probability$\frac{a^2+b^2-k}{k^2-k}$.


Ok, let's see how we get that.

First, examine the probability that we get a pair of $a$. The probability of the first book being $a$ would be $\left(\frac{a}{k}\right)$. Ok! Now, let's find the probability of the next book being $a$. Since we've already chosen a book, then our probability is $\frac{a-1}{k-1}$. So, our probability of choosing both $a$s is $\left(\frac{a}{k}\right)\left(\frac{a-1}{k-1}\right)$. Ok, now let's do the same thing that we did to $a$ to $b$. Again, we get $\left(\frac{b}{k}\right)\left(\frac{b-1}{k-1}\right)$, and so our probability is  $$\left(\frac{a}{k}\right)\left(\frac{a-1}{k-1}\right)+\left(\frac{b}{k}\right)\left(\frac{b-1}{k-1}\right)$$Phew! Now, we combine the fractions, to get $\frac{a^2+b^2-a-b}{k^2-k}$. Since $-a-b=-k$, then we finally have $\boxed{\frac{a^2+b^2-k}{k^2-k}}$. Now, you can see that we can extend this to pulling out $d$ books and having even more series! Have fun playing with formulas, expanding, and more!



~moab33

$2)$ Find $\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5+{5+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5}}}}}}}}...$ (There are infinetly many of those square roots).

So, let's start by tackling $1)$. If $\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5}}}}}}}}}}...=p_1$,SolutionWe first notice that since $\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5\sqrt{5}}}}}}}}}}...$ is infinite, we can rewrite it as $\sqrt{5p_1}$. Since $\sqrt{5p_1}=p_1$, we have that $p_1=5, 0$. Since $0$ is clearly not positive, $p_1=5$. In general, $\sqrt{z\sqrt{z\sqrt{z\sqrt{z\sqrt{z\sqrt{z\sqrt{z\sqrt{z\sqrt{z}}}}}}}}}...=z$. (Remember that the square roots are infinite!)




Now, let's tackle $2)$.

If $\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5{+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5}}}}}}}}...=p_2$, SolutionRewriting this gives $\sqrt{5+p}=p$. Uh oh! Luckily, we know quadratics! $$\sqrt{5+p}=p\rightarrow 5+p=p^2\rightarrow p^2-p-5=0$$. Good! Now, we use the quadratic formula. $\frac{1\pm\sqrt{21}}{2}$.


I'm a bit unsure about $2)$, so I'd like you to check for me. Also, as a challenge, can you generalize both of these:

$$\sqrt{k+\sqrt{k+\sqrt{k+\sqrt{k+\sqrt{k+\sqrt{k+\sqrt{k}}}}}}}...=p_2$$$$\sqrt{c-\sqrt{c-{-\sqrt{c-\sqrt{c-\sqrt{c-\sqrt{c-\sqrt{c}}}}}}}}...=p_3$$?

(I'll try to make more of these daily, so stay tuned! Also, I didn't know where I would post this so I decided to put it here. Please tell me if it belongs here!)

topics.title: Lots of Confuzzling Questions
topics.text:
Sup y'all. Hope your day is going great. Now, I'll make it even better by throwing a bunch of math problems at you! These I came across while preparing for MATHCOUNTS States, but I couldn't figure them out. Any help would be greatly appreciated.



(1) For each positive integer $n$ such that $n<10,000$, the number $n+2005$ has exactly 21 positive factors. What is the sum of all the possible values of $n$?

For this one I just tried straight-up bashing and got 911, but that wasn't the correct answer.



(2) When a positive three-digit dividend with a units digit of $2$ is divided by a positive one-digit divisor, the result is a whole-number quotient with a remainder of 1. How many distinct values are possible for this three-digit dividend?

G&C didn't help me here. I got 111, which was incorrect.



(3) What is the sum of all integer values of $n$ such that $\frac{20}{2n-1}$ is an integer?

Don't you just find the factors of 20 and do it? I did, but somehow 4 wasn't the right answer.



(4) Sarah has four decks of 15 cards each. One deck is red, one is blue, one is yellow and one is green. Each deck's cards are numbered 1 through 15. Sara (this is how they wrote it in the competition - typo???) combines all four decks to form one large deck. When selected at random and without replacement, what is the probability that Sarah will first choose a red card with a prime number and then choose a card with a non-prime number on her second selection? Express your answer as a common fraction.

This one I found the probability of the first case, then the probability of the second case, then got $\frac{23}{490}$, which (surprise, surprise!) was wrong.



I have more problems, but I don't want to make your day too happy. I'll just ask these four for now. If you have any hints or suggestions, that would be great.



Enjoy your night!



AlexOg123
